# The research question

Psychology runs on samples, and whether you buy a finding depends partly on who
was actually in the study. When a paper doesn't say what its participants looked
like demographically, you can't really tell how far the claim reaches, and a
later meta-analysis can't tell who the literature is actually speaking for. That's
the sample representativeness question, and it has two sides: a descriptive one
and a change-over-time one.

I'm after both. First, how often do psychology papers actually report participant
demographics (gender, race, education, socioeconomic status)? Second, has that
changed from 2010 to 2026, and does it look different across subfields or across
the COVID-19 disruption?

I stick to one venue, PLOS ONE, to keep things manageable. It's high-volume,
covers lots of fields, and is fully open access, so I can actually pull the whole
corpus and read it by machine instead of hitting paywalls. That's what makes a
study across tens of thousands of articles doable instead of hand-coding a few
hundred.

Hand-coding doesn't scale to that many articles, so I hand the reading off to a
large language model. For each qualifying paper, the model reads the methods text
and gives back the reported demographics in a fixed structured format, which I
then roll up into reporting-rate trends.

## Temporal design

To track change over time I split the window into four periods that line up with
distinct eras:

| Stage | Years | Rationale |
|-------|-------|-----------|
| Early | 2010 to 2014 | Baseline era |
| Middle | 2015 to 2019 | Settled, pre-pandemic |
| COVID | 2020 to 2023 | Pandemic disruption |
| Post-COVID | 2024 to 2026 | Recovery |

# The extraction schema

For every distinct participant sample a paper describes, I code whether each
demographic was reported and how much detail there was:

| Demographic | Coded fields |
|-------------|--------------|
| Gender | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage breakdown (male / female / other) |
| Race | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage breakdown (white / black / hispanic / asian / other) |
| Education | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage with versus without college |
| Socioeconomic status | An ordinal 0/1/2 code: 0 = not reported, 1 = reported only categorically (e.g. "low income"), 2 = reported with a numeric threshold (e.g. below $30,000) |

Two things about the schema are on purpose and they matter.

The unit is the participant sample, not the paper. One paper can report several
separate samples, and I code each as its own row, tied together by the shared
article ID (its DOI). If I squashed a paper's samples into one row I'd throw away
real within-paper variation and skew the reporting-rate numbers.

Each row also carries some article-level metadata: publication date, the
corresponding author's institution, and the full PLOS subject taxonomy for the
paper. Those let me break things down by subgroup and keep track of where each row
came from.

## Inclusion criteria

A paper makes it into the corpus only if it's an empirical research article (not
an editorial, correction, or review), published in PLOS ONE, filed by PLOS under
psychology (any subfield), and dated between 2010 and 2026. I don't set any
minimum sample size.

# Pipeline architecture

The whole thing is a straight line of stages, each one producing something the
next stage eats:

```
1. Enumerate qualifying psychology articles  ->  master index (58,467 articles)  [DONE]
2. Draw a stratified pilot sample            ->  46 articles                      [DONE]
3. Run the model over the pilot              ->  extracted demographics            [NEXT]
4. Adjudicate pilot accuracy by hand         ->  proceed / revise decision
5. Run the model over the full index         ->  full demographics table
6. Aggregate the table                       ->  reporting-rate trends (the result)
```

Stages 1 and 2 are done and checked. The rest of this doc walks through how I
built them and what the later stages still leave open.

## Computing environment

The pipeline runs on Rivanna, UVA's high-performance computing cluster. Two things
push it there. The model is too big for ordinary hardware and needs several
high-memory GPUs at once. And the full extraction over 58,467 articles is
embarrassingly parallel, so I split it across a lot of workers to finish in a
reasonable amount of wall-clock time. The orchestration is written to survive
preemption and lost sessions, since individual jobs run for hours.

# Decision 1: data acquisition

This was the biggest design call, and the reasoning is worth writing out in full,
because I only landed on the final setup after my first approach ran into the
realities of the corpus. I started with one plan, hit four separate problems, and
ended up somewhere different and more defensible.

## The initial approach: bulk local corpus

PLOS hands out an open dataset, allofplos, with every PLOS article as a JATS XML
file. I pulled the whole thing: roughly 391,000 articles, about 9 GB compressed,
sitting on the cluster. Each file has not just the article text but PLOS's nested
subject taxonomy, encoded as tags:

```
Biology and life sciences  ->  Psychology  ->  Social psychology
```

The appeal was self-containment: parse the taxonomy out of each file, keep the
psychology articles, and never depend on a network service again. My parser went
straight to the subfield sitting one level under a "Psychology" node:

```python
def get_psychology_subfields(article):
    """Return the psychology subfield(s) an article is tagged with.
    e.g. Biology > Psychology > Social psychology  ->  ["Social psychology"]
    """
    subfields = []
    for node in article.subject_nodes:
        if node.text == "Psychology":
            # grab the tag(s) nested one level under Psychology
            subfields.extend(child.text for child in node.children)
    return subfields
```

## Problem A: taxonomy schema drift

My first version returned zero psychology articles. I tracked it down by dumping
the raw taxonomy block from a few recent articles and just reading it. The tags
were there, but the container around them had been renamed. PLOS labels each
taxonomy block with a type attribute; older articles use "Discipline", newer ones
use "Discipline-v3". My parser was matching the exact string "Discipline", so it
quietly dropped every modern article.

The fix was to match any type that starts with "Discipline", which covers both.
The bigger lesson, which kept coming up, is that PLOS's encoding hasn't stayed put
across fifteen years of publishing, so I check structural assumptions against the
corpus instead of a single example.

## Problem B: subfield vocabulary mismatch

The original plan named five target subfields: social, cognitive, developmental,
clinical, and quantitative psychology. Checking against the corpus turned up two
mismatches. PLOS's controlled vocabulary has no "Quantitative psychology" term at
all, so that one would have matched nothing. And PLOS uses several subfields the
plan didn't list, like Experimental psychology, Psychometrics, Behavior, and
Emotions.

Instead of forcing a preset list the taxonomy doesn't honor, I decided to keep all
the subfields. So the design became taxonomy-driven: I keep every article PLOS
files under Psychology and record whatever subfield term PLOS gave it, regardless
of the original five. That stays true to how the field organizes itself and lets
me group or subset by subfield later. In the finished corpus that's 23 subfields,
not five:

Addiction, Applied psychology, Behavior, Cognitive psychology, Collective human
behavior, Developmental psychology, Emotions, Experimental psychology, Gender
identity, Instinct, Neuropsychology, Pain psychology, Personality, Psychological
adjustment, Psychological attitudes, Psychological defense mechanisms,
Psychological stress, Psychology (unspecified), Psychometrics, Psychophysics,
Relaxation (psychology), Sexual identity, and Social psychology.

The range is worth noticing. Some are standard subfields (social, cognitive,
developmental psychology), some are broad topic areas PLOS files under Psychology
(Behavior, Emotions), and a few are narrow or barely about human participants at
all (Instinct, plus animal-behavior work PLOS still tags under Psychology).
Whether to analyze all 23 or narrow to a defined core is one of the open questions
at the end.

## Problem C: the 2015 discontinuity

With the taxonomy parsing correctly, I ran the full scan over all 391,000 files
and built a first master index. A routine check, counting psychology articles per
year, turned up a gap that no real-world mechanism could explain as signal:

```
2014: 2,002 articles
2015:    12 articles    <- implausible
2016: 2,100 articles
```

A near-empty year sitting between two full ones screams bug, not trend, so I dug
in instead of moving on.

My first guess was date parsing: maybe 2015 articles were getting misdated and
shoved into neighboring years. I ruled that out by building a year histogram over
all PLOS ONE articles regardless of subject, which showed 2015 fully populated
with correctly dated articles. The articles were there and dated fine; they just
weren't being recognized as psychology.

My second guess pinned it on subject detection in 2015. I set up a per-year
comparison between how many articles my parser tagged as psychology and how many
just had the substring "psych" somewhere in their raw tags (the counts below are
what I saw at the time):

```
year | total articles | tagged psychology | contains "psych"
2014 |      594       |        37         |         38
2015 |      561       |         1         |          1
2016 |      435       |        35         |         35
```

That settled it. For 2015 even the dumb substring search found basically nothing,
which meant those articles had no subject taxonomy at all, not taxonomy in some
weird shape. Dumping the raw taxonomy block from a bunch of 2015 articles and
tallying the type attributes across the year confirmed it: almost every 2015
article had only

```xml
<article-categories>
  <subj-group subj-group-type="heading">
    <subject>Research Article</subject>
  </subj-group>
</article-categories>
```

a bare document-class heading and no subject taxonomy whatsoever. The count was
clear: of 561 sampled 2015 articles, 557 had no subject tags in their distributed
files, and so did about 37% of 2013 articles.

This is a property of the data PLOS ships, not a bug in my code. PLOS classified
these articles in its own systems but, for that stretch, never wrote the taxonomy
into the downloadable files. You can't read a label that was never written. Left
uncorrected, this would have wiped out most of 2015 and a good chunk of 2013,
which would blow up the Middle stage and any trend line crossing that stretch.

## The resolution: Solr for discovery

The taxonomy is missing from the files PLOS distributes, but not from PLOS itself.
PLOS runs a Solr search index that has the real subject classification for every
article, including the ones whose files leave it out. So I flipped the
architecture around: use the search index to figure out which articles qualify
(discovery), and keep the local files just for the full text the model has to
read. That split, search index for discovery and local corpus for full text, is
actually what the original plan proposed before I went for the bulk-local
shortcut.

## Problem D: query construction

Getting the discovery query right took two more fixes, each of which I isolated by
adding one constraint at a time and watching the result count.

First, the index has way more than whole articles in it; it also indexes pieces
like sections and figures. Without a specific `doc_type:full` filter, the query
comes back with several million of those fragments instead of articles. Second,
the constraints have to go in as strict filter queries. A loosely written query
gets read loosely by the endpoint and hands back basically the whole date range
instead of just the psychology subset.

With both fixes in, each constraint narrows the count sensibly:

```
q=*:* only                  : 3,487,529   (all indexed units, incl. fragments)
+ doc_type:full             :   411,419   (whole articles, all journals)
+ journal:"PLOS ONE"        :   332,150
+ article_type Research     :   313,425
+ date = 2015               :    28,107   (PLOS ONE research articles, 2015)
+ subject Psychology        :     4,346   (2015 psychology, recovered)
```

The actual query is a bunch of filters AND-ed together:

```python
filters = [
    'doc_type:full',                       # essential: whole articles only
    'journal:"PLOS ONE"',
    'article_type:"Research Article"',
    'subject:"Psychology"',
    f'publication_date:[{year}-01-01T00:00:00Z TO {year}-12-31T23:59:59Z]',
]
```

With the search-index approach, 2015 jumped from 12 articles to 4,346. The index
gives each subject as a full path, like /Biology and life
sciences/Psychology/Cognitive psychology/Language, and I read the subfield off as
the segment right after "Psychology", which keeps the same meaning as the earlier
XML parser.

## Operational issues of note

Two cluster-specific problems came up too, both the kind that quietly eat your
time when they aren't written down.

Batch jobs kept failing with a missing-dependency error even though the software
was installed. Turned out the usual command for activating the software
environment behaves differently inside a non-interactive batch job than in an
interactive shell; it looked like it worked but left the job pointed at the wrong
interpreter. I fixed it by calling the right interpreter by its absolute path and
skipping activation entirely.

Separately, a long-running preprocessing step I kicked off in the background of a
terminal kept getting killed whenever the connection dropped, because the web
terminal tears down its process group when the session ends. Now I submit that
work as a scheduled job so it runs on its own, independent of any terminal. Both
fixes are baked into the run scripts.

## Data-quality handling

The pipeline puts up with two problems I saw in the corpus. One article file was
truncated and wouldn't parse; the scanner logs it and skips it rather than killing
a multi-hour job over one bad file out of 391,000. And about 6% of the articles
the search index returns, mostly recent 2025 and 2026 papers, aren't in the local
file snapshot, so there's no full text to pull; I flag those and leave them out of
sampling so the pipeline never tries to code an article it can't read.

# The finished master index

With the search-index approach the per-year counts are smooth, with no leftover
gap:

```python
total: 58,467 psychology articles
by year:
  2010:  853   2014: 4,249   2018: 3,492   2022: 3,761
  2011: 1,886  2015: 4,346   2019: 3,219   2023: 3,761
  2012: 2,481  2016: 3,663   2020: 3,548   2024: 4,249
  2013: 4,478  2017: 3,367   2021: 3,714   2025: 5,009
                                            2026: 2,391 (partial year)
by stage:
  early: 13,947   middle: 18,087   covid: 14,784   post-covid: 11,649
```

The lower 2010 count is just PLOS ONE publishing less back then, a real feature of
the venue, not an artifact. The 2026 count is partial because the year isn't over.

# Decision 2: the pilot sample

Before committing to a full run, I try the model out on a small batch and check
the output by hand. Two things about the sampling design matter.

The sample is stratified, not simple random. A plain random draw would be
dominated by high-volume subfields like social and cognitive psychology and might
skip the rarer ones entirely, but the whole point of the pilot is to poke the
model across the full range of writing styles. So I take two articles from each
subfield in the index.

The draw is reproducible. It's seeded with a fixed value, so I can regenerate the
exact same sample, which is table stakes for anything transparent and auditable.

```python
def stratified_sample(articles, per_subfield=2, seed=42):
    rng = random.Random(seed)                     # fixed seed = reproducible
    picked = []
    for subfield in all_subfields(articles):      # every subfield present
        candidates = [a for a in articles if subfield in a.subfields]
        if len(candidates) >= per_subfield:       # skip subfields with too few
            picked += rng.sample(candidates, per_subfield)
    return picked
```

The actual sample comes out to 46 articles across the 23 subfields listed earlier.

# Decision 3: model selection

The original plan gave me two candidate models to choose from:

| | Mistral-7B | Llama-3.3-70B (selected) |
|---|---|---|
| Scale | 7 billion parameters | 70 billion parameters |
| Structured-extraction accuracy | Lower; more prone to omission and fabrication | Higher; more reliable |
| Compute cost | Modest; runs on limited hardware | Substantial; requires multiple high-end GPUs |

I went with Llama-3.3-70B. Accuracy is the deciding factor, because a missed or
made-up demographic value feeds straight into the reporting-rate numbers that are
the whole output of the study. Running on Rivanna takes compute cost off the
table, which is the only thing that would push toward the smaller model. The pilot
is there precisely to test whether that pick holds up before the full run.

# Extraction mechanics

I hand each article's text to the model with an instruction that pins down both
what to extract and the output format:

```text
You are coding a psychology research article for a systematic review of
demographic reporting. For EACH distinct participant sample, code the four
demographics defined by the schema above (gender, race, education,
socioeconomic status), and for each one, whether it was reported and, where
reported, its breakdown.

Respond with ONLY a JSON array, one element per sample, with these exact keys...
```

Two safeguards keep the output honest. It's schema-validated, so a response has to
be well-formed structured data with exactly the required fields; anything
malformed gets rejected and flagged instead of quietly slipping into the dataset.
And I move the methods and participants sections to the front of the text I send,
since that's where demographics live, which puts the useful signal near the start
of the prompt for long articles.

# Scaling the full run

Pushing 58,467 articles through a 70-billion-parameter model is heavy. I split the
work into independent shards that run at the same time across a lot of GPUs. Each
shard writes its own output file, and the run is safe to restart: an interrupted
shard skips the articles it already finished and picks up from there, which is
essential for multi-hour jobs that can get preempted.

# Aggregation and inference

Once the demographics table is done, the last stage computes two things for each
demographic, for each year, and separately for each of the four stages. The
reporting rate is the share of samples that report a given demographic. The mean
composition is, for instance, the average percentage female among the samples that
reported gender. Tracking those from 2010 to 2026 is the study's answer: whether
demographic reporting in psychology is getting better, and how the path differs
across the early, middle, COVID, and post-COVID periods.

# Reproducibility

All the code and docs are version-controlled on GitHub (SJ-Jain-systems/Halle).
Each stage is its own testable module:

```
src/
  solr_client.py          discovery via the PLOS Solr search index
  build_index_solr.py     materialize the master index of 58,467 articles
  jats_xml.py             parse metadata and full text from the article files
  sample_articles.py      draw the stratified pilot sample
  extract_demographics.py the model instruction and schema validation
  model_backend.py        model execution on the GPUs (vLLM / transformers)
  run_pipeline.py         full run, sharded and restartable
  analyze_trends.py       reporting-rate aggregation by year and stage
docs/
  DECISIONS.md            the three decisions, with full reasoning
  RUNNING_ON_RIVANNA.md   step-by-step run instructions for the cluster
  SCORING_RUBRIC.md       the pilot adjudication rubric
scripts/                  the diagnostics that isolated the 2015 gap and more
tests/                    33 automated tests over the non-model logic
```

Two things worth flagging for anyone auditing this. The non-model logic is covered
by 33 automated tests across parsing, filtering, sampling, and aggregation; the
model itself gets checked by hand-coding the pilot. And the diagnostic scripts
that pinned down the schema drift and the 2015 gap are still in the repo, so the
evidence behind each design call is there to inspect.

# Open questions

Three calls would benefit from a second opinion before the full run.

1. Subfield scope. The taxonomy gives 23 psychology subfields, some broad
   (Behavior, Emotions) and some barely about human participants (say
   animal-behavior work filed under Psychology, or Instinct). Do I analyze all 23,
   or narrow to a defined core of human-participant subfields, and if so which?

2. Coverage at the edges. Pre-2011 articles use the older tagging generation, and
   some 2025 to 2026 articles have no local full text. Are the earliest and latest
   years complete enough for a fair long-term comparison, or should I bound the
   window (say 2011 to 2024)?

3. Validation threshold. How accurate does the pilot have to be, measured against
   the scoring rubric, to justify going ahead with the full run, and who does the
   hand-coding?
